Article | November 13, 2026 Set Your Own Intensity: When You Need More From Your Facility Source: Cytiva When buffer demand grows, the instinctive fix is a bigger kitchen, more hold tanks, or extra storage. That response keeps the same operating model: make it, store it, move it. This article starts from a different question: which part of the buffer workflow is actually holding the facility back? It separates constraints in tanks and labor, holding space, liquid movement, and utility capacity, then shows how inline dilution and inline conditioning change the picture depending on whether they sit in a central kitchen or at the point of use. It also includes a modeling study of a three-step monoclonal antibody process, with figures on liquid volume and floor space. Examine the modeled results to see how much room a different buffer approach can open. Access The Article! Log In Subscribe to access the full article FREE! Article | November 13, 2026 Set Your Own Intensity: When You Need More Output Source: Cytiva A larger bioreactor is the conventional answer to an output limit, but it is not the only one. Intensified fed-batch and production perfusion both raise output from the volume already in place, and neither is inherently the better choice. This article compares high-seed and high-cell-density fed-batch with steady-state and changing-trajectory perfusion, drawing on CHO and monoclonal antibody studies and on 50 L and 200 L perfusion data. It argues that the useful measure is productive biomass, not peak cell density, and that added titer matters only if harvest, capture, purification, and buffer supply can handle it. A larger bioreactor is the conventional answer to an output limit, but it is not the only one. Intensified fed-batch and production perfusion both raise output from the volume already in place, and neither is inherently the better choice. This article compares high-seed and high-cell-density fed-batch with steady-state and changing-trajectory perfusion, drawing on CHO and monoclonal antibody studies and on 50 L and 200 L perfusion data. It argues that the useful measure is productive biomass, not peak cell density, and that added titer matters only if harvest, capture, purification, and buffer supply can handle it. Explore the comparison to see how to match an operating model to your process and facility.
